question.:question/problem: $-5\left(\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
-5\left(\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)=-5\left(\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)
$$

We then use the fact that ${cot}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
-5\left(\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x\right)
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left(\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{csc}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{cos}^{3}⁡x+{cot}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}({cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{3}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{csc}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Calculate $-5\left(\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
-5\left(\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)=-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

We then use the fact that $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left(\int \frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{8{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int {tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int {(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left(3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4}\right)\\  & =-5\left(3[\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡0]\right)\\  & =-5\left(3(\sqrt{2}-1)\right)\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: $-5\left(\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
-5\left(\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)=-5\left(\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)
$$

We then use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}=\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ to express this as

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left(\int \operatorname{cot}⁡x(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(\int (\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\int (\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left(\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left(\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x\right)\\  & =-5\left(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\right)+C\\  & =-5\left(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡4x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x\right)=-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cot}⁡4x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡4x}\,\text{d}x\right)
$$

Then, we use the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡4x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}$ and $\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡4x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡4x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡4x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=4x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=4x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{4}(sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2})-sin\,(0))\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{4}(1-0)\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

The original quotient is undefined at $x=0$. This is an improper integral; the simplified integrand has a finite right limit there.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left({\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡3x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡3x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\right)&=-5\left({\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=3x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.$ 

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=3x.$

| $x$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ | $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\left({\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\right)& =-5\left({\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))\right)\\  & =-5\left(\frac{1}{3}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\right)\\  & =-5\left(0\right)\end{aligned}
